newsitem.title: JAPAN: Falling Nikkei fuels fears of foreign sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Falling Nikkei fuels fears of foreign sell-off.

text.p: The falling dollar-denominated value of Japan's benchmark Nikkei share average has fuelled fears in the market that foreign investors may soon start to dump their Japanese stock holdings, analysts said on Tuesday.

In dollar terms the Nikkei now stands just below $150, which brokers said was the average level at which foreign investors have bought Japanese stocks since 1992. Some brokers said this could spur foreign investors to unload their Japanese stock holdings in order to limit their losses.
"There are still fears about foreign investors selling, and we are still cautious," said Harushige Kobayashi, deputy general manager at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd.
"But I expect the Nikkei to drift between 17,000 and 18,000 for now," he added.
On Tuesday, the Nikkei 225 average closed at 17,358.16 yen, or $147.35 based on a dollar rate of 117.80 yen in late Tokyo trade on Tuesday.
"Some (foreign) investors will definitely sell Japanese equities" in order to limit potential losses on their Japan stock holdings, said Shinichi Ichikawa, a strategist at Credit Lyonnais Securities.

He said the dollar's recent rally above 115 yen was expected to have a negative impact on import-oriented Japanese companies, weaken Japan's economic fundamentals and spur foreign investors to sell shares in order to cut their losses.

But other analysts downplayed the risk of foreign sales, arguing that foreign investors were reaping substantial profits from U.S. and other overseas stocks which would mitigate pressure to liquidate any losing positions in the Japanese market.
"Since other foreign shares have risen so much, it is hard to imagine that foreign investors would dump their Japanese equities holdings immediately," said Yamaichi's Kobayashi.

Another broker said foreign investors would be digging their own graves if they began dumping Japanese shares, since a mass exodus of foreigners would spark a further tumble in share prices and add to their potential losses.
